The Women's International League for Peace and Freedom är en global kvinnorättsorganisation som grundades 1915. WILPF arbetar för att uppnå feministisk fred för jämlikhet, rättvisa och en avmilitariserad säkerhet genom en tudelad men sammankopplad ansats: genom att adressera grundorsaker till våld med en feministik ansats och genom att mobilisera för ickevåldsam aktion. WILPF är en medlemsbaserad organisation med aktiva sektioner i 42 länder världen runt, men fungerar även som en icke-statlig organisation med programsamarbeten i till exempel MENA-regionen. Sida föreslås ge kärnstöd till WILPF:s internationella sekretariat i Geneve baserat på WILPF:s internationella strategi för 2017-19.

The Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom is a global women's rights organisation, which was founded in 1915. WILPF works to advance feminist peace for equality, justice, and demilitarised security by way of two interlinked paths: by addressing the root causes of violence with a feminist lens and by mobilising for nonviolent action. WILPF is a membership organization with active sections in 42 countries around the world, but also functions as an NGO with programmatic collaborations in for example the MENA region. Sida provides core support to the WILPF International Secretariat in Geneva based on the WILPF International Strategy 2017-19.

description.narrative:
In this final report for the period 2017-2021 there is an initial section compiling some longer-term results. Some of them stem from the Sida commissioned evaluation Evaluation of Womens International League for Peace and Freedom (WILPF), Core Support 20172021 (Dox 027889/21 and Sida´s statement on the evaluation Dox 042952/21), and others have been added. From Sida´s perspective, one of the major strength of WILPF is its ability to combine a qualified and informed feminist global outreach advocacy with grass root activism. The increased sub-granting is also perceived as a good step to build the national and local movements, as well as increase global legitimacy, and thereby interconnect the entire organisation.
Below are a few examples of achievements with a higher degree of overall impact:
In terms of influence - the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN) of the treaty-based prohibition resulted in a Nobel Peace Prize in 2017 after 122 governments voted for the Treaty adoption at the United Nations General Assembly. This was the result of nearly a decade of work for WILPF and its partners of which WILPF is an active and a Steering Group member, in recognition of the collective work to achieve the Treaty. WILPFs visibility, voice, and persistence over time produce a constant voice and show a high-level of impact and the power of partnerships in order to gain legally bound changes for human security. WILPF also used a lot of advocacy efforts to ensure the two new Security Council Resolutions on Women, Peace and Security (WPS) adopted in 2019 (UNSCR 2467 and UNSCR 2493) moved the WPS Agenda forward and did not roll back existing commitments (which was an overarching risk at the time).
At country levels WILPF has increasingly integrated the feminist political economic analysis (as a tool) in country submissions to human rights mechanisms. This includes: CESCR on Ukraine; CEDAW Committee on Zimbabwe; and Universal Periodic Review (UPR) on Lebanon as well as Submission to CEDAW on general recommendations on trafficking in women and girls in the context of global migration.
WILPFs National Action Plan monitoring page, found on the peacewomen.org, continues to be a well-known resource for WPS practitioners and now also consolidates resources on national- level implementation of the WPS agenda into one place. Each year WILPF publishes its WPS Scorecard, which monitors the activities of the permanent five members of the UNSC on the WPS agenda, thus contributing to enhance accountability.
WILPF supported partners and members from at least six countries (Afghanistan, Cameroon, Colombia, Libya, Syria, Yemen) to brief the UN Secuiry Council, thereby bringing local analysis and amplifying the voice of women to international spaces to speak truth to power. The incorporation of gender and feminist analysis has influened mandate renewals and outputs of the work of UNs highest body. For example, in 2021, 31per cent of the total number of resolutions adopted included gender considerations, compared to 15 per cent in 2017.
In terms of strengthening human security in the MENA region the International Secretariat of WILPF contributed to enhancing capacities of partners to engage with duty bearers in MENA, including providing high level technical advisory and accompanied partners in drafting and submitting to human rights instruments and treaty bodies. In Yemen, concretely, sexual violence was brought into the international limelight. For instance, the Security Council Resolution 2564 (2021) condemned conflict-related sexual violence in Houthi-controlled areas. This was the culmination of efforts exerted by grass root organisations, including Peace Track Initiative-Yemens work in integrating gender.
In response to the UN Secretary-General´s appeal for a global ceasefire in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the feminist FIRE consortium (in which WILPF is a member together with Kvinna till kvinna and MADRE) developed five feminist principles to serve as the foundation for the negotiation, design, and implementation of meaningful ceasefires.
In terms of participation during the peace process in Colombia, WILPF was active when more than 100 provisions on gender, including on zero tolerance on sexual and gender-based violence were integrated into the peace agreement based on women civil societys recommendations. In 2018, WILPF ensured that references to gender-based violence, gendered impact of small arms and womens participation were made in a report adopted by the UN Programme for Action on small arms and light weapons. This language contributes to mainstreaming of gender in small arms control and is a concrete result of WILPFs joint advocacy work with other civil society organisations.
There are numerous examples of participation in the global-local arenas are enhancing voice of local women peace builders:
- Overall, WILPF reports that it contributed to an increase in the number of women Civil Society briefers at the UN Security Council (UNSC). Between 2017-2021, there were 163 women Civil Society briefers at the Council, 46 of whom were facilitated by the coalition the NGO Working Group (NGOWG) on WPS, with WILPF directly supporting 25 women;
- WILPF Cameroon created a Womens Consultation Platform in 2019 to ensure womens voices were adequately reflected in the National Dialogue process. Following consultations in all regions and with Diaspora, a memorandum and advocacy document were developed reflecting womens concerns.
- WILPF in Colombia was part of the delegation to Commission of th Status of Women (CSW) and participated in CEDAW review of Colombia and contributed to the National Development Plan, including holding bilateral meetings with government officials and UN;
- WILPF DRC has played a key role in bringing domestic violence to the UPR and the CEDAW Committee when most NGOs tend to focus on sexual violence in conflict.
But also where national and local outreach, based on a globally developed WILPF model, can enhance participation:
- WILPF Nigeria's work on "Women Situation Room" expanded and implemented activities in 9 states and built capacity of 70 women leaders to strengthen womens political participation in peace processes, including election monitoring.
Some contributions in 2021
WILPF has a very broad set of activities and achievements, and it is not possible to capture them all here. A selection of achievements include:
During 2021, the taliban take over in Afghanistan, and the subsequent steep back-lash for gender equality, overshadows other country contexts. WILPF has been active throughout as it has an active Section in the country, which even before the power overturn, needed increased protection and later be part of the evacuation schemes. WILPF pushed for women participation in the previous peace process, it mobilised the international civil society and was part of pushing for the installment of a Special rapporteur function and a Commission of Inquiry.
In terms of thematic evolvement, climate and environment have increasingly emerged as a new and important area of work, particularly with the synergies and connections between militarism and the environment. WILPF participated in COP26; led a campaign for nuclear abolition around the Hiroshima and Nagasaki anniversaries; supported Sections engagement and participation in these international mechanisms and through small grants; developed a website on Feminism, Gender and Environment.
The International Secretariat continued to build demand driven thematic capacity for its sections, groups and partners in order to enhance engagement within civil society spaces and with the UN system on UPR processes, advocacy with UN human rights mechanisms, gender-sensitive human rights research and, additionally, provided financial grants. Two new Groups joined in 2021: WILPF Austria and WILPF Guinea.
In 2021, WILPF reports that it continued to raise the profile of weapons issues within human rights fora and disarmament spaces including a submission to the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) examining the human rights impact of firearms on children and youth; submissions to the UN Human Rights Committee about human rights, arms transfers, and nuclear weapons; a submission to the UN CEDAW Committee on the use of arms in internal repression and the impacts of surveillance technologies; and a submission to the UN Working Group on Mercenaries regarding the human rights implications of cyber mercenaries.
As being relevant to Sweden and the initiative to hold a high level meeting on peace building financing, it could be of particular interest to high light WILPF´s collaborative efforts, with five INGOs (GPPAC, ICAN, KtK, GWNP, and Madre), to collectively influence donors, governments and UN plans on financing peace building. These efforts resulted in a joint background paper that focuses on six structural barriers faced by diverse women peace builders in accessing funds to support their work, which has since been used for high level meeting advocacy during 2022.
